division.heading: Request for Particulars, Amendments to Pleadings and Close of Pleadings

operative_text.controlling:
3.61(1)  A party on whom a pleading is served may serve on the
party who served the pleading a request for particulars about
anything in the pleading.
(2)  If the requesting party does not receive a sufficient response
within 10 days after the date on which the request is served, the
requesting party may apply to the Court for an order requiring the
party who served the pleading to provide the particulars.
(3)  If the Court orders particulars to be provided, it must specify a
time within which the order is to be complied with.
(4)  Subject to any order, despite a request for particulars, the
obligation under these rules to file and serve pleadings continues
even though a request for particulars has been made and whether or
not it has been complied with.

commentary.text: Rule 3.61 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.61. 1. When Available Particulars generally will not be ordered after the close of pleadings and before discovery. The timing of this application also gives me some difficulty. While the primary purpose of particulars is to enable to the other side to defend, particulars may also serve to narrow the issues, prevent surprise at trial and save time. To accomplish this, particulars may be ordered after the close of the pleadings. (See Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v. British Columbia Electric Co. Ltd., supra; Okalta Oils Limited v. Alberta Petroleum Consolidated Limited, [1935] 2 W.W.R. 664 (Alta. S.C.); Odgers on Pleading and Practice (21st Ed.), p. 149). In my view, the law on this point is correctly summarized in Canadian Encyclopedic Digest (Western, 2nd Ed.), vol. 17, at para. 106, as follows: Particulars are ordered primarily with a view of having the prior pleading made sufficiently distinct to enable the applicant for particulars to frame his answer properly. If the pleadings are closed particulars cannot be required for that purpose, but, notwithstanding the pleadings are closed, particulars may be ordered, in a proper case, for the purpose of saving expense, or for the purpose of preventing surprise at the trial. The proper principle is to order particulars only when, from the nature of the case, they are necessary to limit the inquiry, or are necessary by reason of matters brought forward on affidavit. It is now well-settled practice that particulars after pleading will not be ordered until after discovery; following this principle further, if discovery results in full disclosure, particulars are not necessary; if discovery does not result in full disclosure particulars will be ordered. It follows that discovery takes the place of particulars if it results in full disclosure. To justify an order for particulars after the close of the pleadings, it must be shown by affidavit, or otherwise, that they are necessary for the purpose of saving expense or preventing surprise at the trial. Such an order should not be made as of course. Oceatain Investments Ltd. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 (Q.B.), at 366-67, per McFadyen J. (approved by Prowse J. in Magrath Market Place Ltd. v. 401624 Alberta Inc. (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 94 at 96 (Q.B.)). Particulars may be ordered after examinations for discovery if that process has been unsuccessful in providing the information: This is not the usual case of a party applying for particulars. The pleadings are closed and the plaintiff was content to go to discoveries with the pleas as they stand. The plaintiff expected to get better particulars on discovery. If he had got what he wanted on discoveries this application would not have been made. A party cannot say that better particulars of his pleas should not be given because the pleadings are closed, and also say that better particulars should not be given on discoveries. That reduces itself to saying that better particulars should not be given at any time. The other party must wait to trial to see what the particulars are. That of course would not be acceptable. The fact that the defendant has refused to give more particulars at its examination is a special circumstance to justify the ordering of particulars if the pleading is deficient in that regard. Here discovery of the officer has not resulted in full disclosure so particulars should be ordered: Oceatain Investments v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 (Q.B.) …Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 (Master), at 257, per Master Funduk. 2. Entitlement to Particulars Defendants are entitled to particulars even if the defendant has the information. Counsel for the plaintiff submits that the defendants have knowledge of how this figure is arrived at as they were formerly his solicitors. I do not believe that this is an appropriate position. The plaintiff is advancing a claim for loss of income against the defendants. They are entitled to know how he arrives at that amount. Kully v. Decore (1981), 34 A.R. 617 at 620 (Master). In Stoney Tribal Council v. R., 2005 ABCA 204, 2005 CarswellAlta 773, 54 Alta. L.R. (4th) 184, the Court said, at pp. 185-186: The appellant (the new defendant) formally demanded a number of particulars of the amended statement of claim. The respondent plaintiffs refused to provide almost all the particulars demanded, alleging in each case that they were “evidence in the possession and control of the Defendants” or the like. The reply to demand for particulars did not allege that the appellant (the new defendant) had such knowledge. It is admitted that the appellant was incorporated about 70 years after the C.P.R.'s original line was built. In any event, the fact that a defendant knows the facts is not a legal objection to the plaintiff's giving particulars. That is because particulars are pleadings and claims, not discovery or evidence. For example, the defendant driver in a highway collision suit was present at the collision and saw it all, but he is still entitled to particulars of the plaintiff's plea of negligence. The defendant may know what he actually did, but he does not know what the plaintiff thinks that the defendant did. It is no objection to an application for particulars that the applicant must know the true facts of the case better than his opponent. He is entitled to know the outline of the case that his adversary will try to make against him, which may be something very different from the true facts of the case. • Goulding, Simon, Odgers on Civil Court Actions, p. 215, 24th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1996) And if a statement of claim covers a large topic or more than one specified transaction, the defendant does not know which of the many things which he has done is in issue. Nor whether the complaint is something which someone else did, or no one did. The question is one of natural justice: notice of the claim which the defendant has to meet. We are persuaded by the reasoning to like effect in Kully v. Decore (1981), 34 A.R. 617 (Alta. Q.B.), 620 (M.) (para. 7), and in Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 (Alta. Master), 255-6 (M.) (para. 29). (There is a contrary statement in Misericordia Hospital v. Acres Consulting Services Ltd. (1977), 5 A.R. 254 (Alta. T.D.), but it gives no reasoning and cites Patterson v. Canadian Pacific Railway (1917), [1918] 1 W.W.R. 40 (Alta. C.A.). That case is not on point, and very likely pp. 45-46 of it have been misread.) If the provision of particulars will unduly delay the action, the court may decline to order them. In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead. However, this case is unique, from the point of view of the number of defendants, the complexity of the the issues involved, the quantum of damages claimed and the massive quantities of relevant documents (estimated by the plaintiffs to be in the neighbourhood of two million pages). I accept the plaintiff's argument that if they were required to supply exhaustive particulars at this stage, the proceedings would be substantially delayed, perhaps by as much as one year. No one would be able to proceed with discovery of documents or examinations for discovery until the plaintiffs had completed and finalized their list of particulars… I also agree with the defendants' submission that examination for discovery are no substitute for particulars, since one of the functions of particulars is to narrow the issues and thus circumscribe the scope of discoveries. There is a danger that the defendants will be put to unnecessary time and expense in they are not given complete particulars at this stage. However, there is an overriding factor in the litigation. Because of the magnitude of the alleged liability, I am certain that each defendant will conduct thorough and lengthy discoveries. After examining all the material before me, I am satisfied that all defendants are presently in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 366-67, per Wachowich J. Justice Wachowich's decision in Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), should not be taken as authority to provide only partial particulars when consequential delay is not an issue. In 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v. Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151, the Plaintiff sought “damages and other relief against Mr. Bazinet and four other Defendants, for loss of business revenue due to alleged activities of the Defendants which allegedly sought to harm the reputation of the Plaintiff. Specifically, the Plaintiff [alleged] improper use of the Plaintiff's confidential information and trade secrets.” The Defendant Bazinet demanded particulars. The Plaintiff filed and served a Notice to Admit Facts. In the Plaintiff's reply to the Defendant's demand for particulars, the Plaintiff used the phrase “includes but not limited to”. Justice Schutz did not approve the use of that phrase: 37 As for the phrase “includes but not limited to”, Wachowich J expresses concern about this qualifier in Canadian Commercial Bank, and notes that questioning is not a substitute for particulars. In that case, however, Wachowich J did not order further particulars because he was satisfied that “… all Defendants are at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on with what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process”: Canadian Commercial Bank at para 33. 38 The Plaintiff must give the Defendant particulars of what the Plaintiff knows. Mr. Bazinet is not obliged to speculate, or guess, about what the Plaintiff knows. Accordingly, the Plaintiff shall remove references to what the Defendant “knows” and replace those references with such further or other particulars upon which the Plaintiff intends to rely in its case against Mr. Bazinet. 39 Further, the phrase “including but not limited to” shall not form part of the Plaintiff's pleadings. I agree that in the face of an allegation “including but not limited to”, questioning cannot and shall not be a substitute for particulars, and I am not able to find that Mr. Bazinet is at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable him to sufficiently plead his defence or prepare evidence for questioning, or trial. 40 Relevance is determined by the pleadings. The Plaintiff's intention to rely on allegations that the Defendant “knows”, or that some allegations are “including but not limited to” other, unstated, unknown allegations, is not fair to the Defendant. The boundaries of the Plaintiff's pleadings must be drawn with sufficient particularity by the Plaintiff that the Defendant is not left to speculate, or guess, about that to which the Plaintiff refers, or about the case the Defendant must meet. 41 I find that the Plaintiff's particulars, to this point, suffer the same frailties as the deficiencies mentioned in Stoney and Caskey and Canadian Commercial Bank: Mr. Bazinet is entitled to know the outline of the case that his adversary will try to make against him, which may be something very different from the true facts of the case. The amended statement of claim covers a large topic and more than one specified transaction. By using phrases such as “on or about [a given date]”, “further particulars of every defamatory statement are available to Bazinet but not [the Plaintiff]”, “further particulars are known to Bazinet”, I agree that it is not possible for Mr. Bazinet to know which of the many things he has done is in in issue. Nor is Mr. Bazinet able to know whether the Plaintiff's complaints are actually about something which someone else did, or no one did. I agree that the fundamental question is one of natural justice: notice of the claim which the defendant has to meet. 3. Purpose of Particulars In Gulf Canada Ltd. v. “Mary Mackin” (The), [1984] 1 F.C. 884, 42 C.P.C. 146, 52 N.R. 282 (C.A.), at 284, Heald J. approved the following as an accurate list of the functions of particulars (as taken from the White Book dealing with English Practice): 1. to inform the other side of the nature of the case they have to meet as distinguished from the mode in which that case is to be proved; 2. to prevent the other side from being taken by surprise at the trial; 3. to enable the other side to know what evidence they ought to be prepared with and to prepare for trial; 4. to limit the generality of the pleadings; 5. to limit and decide the issues to be tried, and as to which discovery is required, and 6. to tie the hands of the party so that he cannot without leave go into any matters not included. Moshansky J., in Welco Expediting Ltd. v. Harris (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 173 (Q.B.), at 181-82, referred with approval to that list. And McFadyen J. stated: The function of particulars is stated in Halsbury's Laws of England (4th Ed.), vol. 36, para. 38, as follows: The function of particulars is to carry into operation the overriding principle that the litigation between the parties, and particularly the trial, should be conducted fairly, openly and without surprises, and incidentally to reduce costs. This function has been variously stated, namely either to limit the generality of the allegations in the pleadings, or to define the issues which have to be tried and for which discovery is required. Each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against him at the trial, and to have such particulars of this opponent's case as will prevent him from being taken by surprise. Particulars enable the other party to decide what evidence he ought to be prepared with and to prepare for the trial. The general rule is that an application for particulars must be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicants' need for particulars. An affidavit is unnecessary where the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident. (See Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v. British Columbia Electric Co. Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 656 (B.C. C.A.) and Steiner v. Lindzon et al. (1976), 1 C.P.C. 237 (Ont. H.C.J.). Oceatain Investments Ltd. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 at 366 (Q.B.). In Alberta v. Altria Group, Inc., 2015 ABQB 390, Justice Strekaf gave this overview of the purpose of particulars and the test to be met in an application for particulars: 14 The purpose of particulars has been discussed in numerous decisions. Any request for particulars should be considered in light of the principle that each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against it at trial. Particulars help to ensure that litigation is conducted fairly, openly, and without surprise. Particulars also help to narrow the scope of the issues to be decided, guide the discovery process, and help to streamline the litigation process. 15 A request for particulars is not akin to an examination for discovery. Particulars function to limit the generality of allegations and to define the issues to be tried, whereas examinations for discovery are to learn the knowledge of the adverse party: Misericordia Hosp v Acres Consulting Services Ltd (1977), 5 AR 254 at 255 (ABSC-TD) (Misericordia). … 17 While not mandatory, an application for particulars should as a general rule be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicant's need for particulars. No substantive affidavits were filed on behalf of any of the Defendants in this case. Therefore, to show that particulars are required, absent an affidavit stating as such, the Defendants must show that the pleading is defective on its face and that “the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident”: Oceatain Investments Ltd v Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 AR 364 (ABQB) at para 8 (Oceatain). 18 The Court has discretion in determining whether the allegations are so vague as to necessitate an order for particulars. As noted by Justice McMahon in Re Indian Residential Schools, 1999 ABQB 823 at para 15: • An order for particulars is discretionary. There are no precise rules as to the degree of particularity required in any given case. Generally, what is reasonable and fair will dictate whether, and to what degree, further particulars will be ordered. 19 Justice McMahon noted that there is a difference between ordering particulars for pleadings and ordering particulars for trial. For an order for particulars in order to plead, the court should ask itself: “are there sufficient facts present to formulate a defence?” This question must be answered with reference to the whole of the Crown's Statement of Claim: see Wesley First Nation v Alberta, 2009 ABQB 418 at para 34 (Wesley First Nation). 20 Pleadings must be succinct, but must still disclose sufficient material facts for the defendant to understand what case it must meet. The amount of detail necessary varies with the nature of each case: William Blake Odgers, Principles of Pleadings and Practice in Civil Actions, 21st ed (London: Stevens & Sons, 1975) at 103. If a specific fact is not set out, but can be properly inferred from other statements in the pleading, that is sufficient for the purposes of a statement of claim: see O'Neill v Rosetown (Town), [1941] 2 WWR 481 (SKCA). 21 Pleadings require facts, but should not contain evidence. The line between these is often difficult to draw: see Can-Air Services Ltd v British Aviation Insurance Co (1988), 63 Alta LR (2d) 61 (CA). Material facts are facts upon which the party pleading relies for its claim, whereas evidence consists of the manner by which those facts are to be proved: Misericordia. The distinction between the two is often a question of degree. Expert report or opinion is evidence, not material fact, and therefore need not be particularized: Hoy v Medtronic, 2004 BCSC 440 at para 39. 22 Finally, requests for particulars that are in the nature of a question of law or of mixed fact and law need not be answered: see Commonwealth Credit Union Ltd v Waylan Mechanical Ltd, 2008 ABQB 96. iv)—Particulars in Complex Cases 23 What degree of particularity is “reasonable and fair” will depend on the circumstances of the case. Various courts have recognized that a realistic and pragmatic approach should be adopted at the pleadings stage in very complex litigation to ensure that these cases are not unduly delayed or prevented from proceeding to trial. This approach is exemplified by the reasoning of the Court of Appeal in Lameman v Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 29 (Lameman): • A plaintiff is required to sufficiently particularize its claim so as to permit the defendants to identify their defenses for the purpose of filing a Statement of defense. However, the demands for particulars should not be permitted to turn into a delaying tactic, or a substitute for what can be obtained through a Notice to Produce Records or the Questioning process Otherwise, litigation will be stonewalled at an early stage through excessive particularization. 24 This approach is reflected in other Alberta cases. In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon held that the court should have a view to the “magnitude and nature of the litigation involved” in determining what, if any, particulars should be ordered: para 16. In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon was considering an application for particulars in a case involving over one thousand actions, over two thousand complainants, and multiple defendants for alleged abuses spanning seven decades. Justice McMahon concluded that, in cases of such size and complexity, “potential delay must be an overriding consideration”: para 18. The courts must adopt a “reasonable and realistic” approach, “seeking fairness for all parties”: paras 16, 21. On one hand, the court should help the parties to narrow the issues as much as possible before discovery. On the other hand, any order for particulars cannot be “so onerous as to prevent Plaintiffs from prosecuting an action which is meritorious …”: para 16. Justice McMahon therefore addressed the issue of potential delay by ordering particulars in a staggered fashion: he ordered broad particulars on a representative basis in order to help the Defendants to frame their defenses and noted that many of the requests would be addressed in discovery. 25 In Wesley First Nation, Justice Martin was similarly considering an application for particulars in a large and complex case where the “claims are extensive, the breaches alleged are numerous, the relevant time frame spans hundreds of years and the territory at issue is vast”: para 2. In this context, Justice Martin endorsed this “realistic” approach at para 23: • While recognizing the need for defendants to understand the case made against them at the pleadings stage, the court must also recognize that not every claim is capable of being pleaded with the same degree of particularity, and that subsequent stages in the litigation process may also function to clarify and narrow the issues. 26 While courts must avoid unduly burdening the plaintiff in its claims, there is a risk that the discovery process will become unwieldy and unnecessarily time-consuming and costly if insufficient particularization is given to the claims. 27 To strike a balance between these competing considerations in large and complex litigation, case management judges “must have some elbow room” in order to “keep the suit moving” and prevent it from being “[bogged] down in interlocutory matters”: Korte v Deloitte, Haskins & Sells (1995), 36 Alta LR (3d) 56 (CA) at para 3. The Court of Appeal in Lameman noted that in complex cases that are case managed, litigation management orders can be more effective than particulars in providing an efficient structure to determine a claim: para 32. 4. Function of Particulars In my view, the guiding principle is that the primary purpose of particulars is to enable the other side to frame a defence. The pleadings should be as succinct as is reasonably possible in order to achieve this end. In Balaz v. Petro-Infor Ltd. (1983), 43 A.R. 229 at 233, the Alberta Court of Appeal dismissed one of a number of applications for further and better particulars in the following way: In my view the allegations with regard to conspiracy, although somewhat vague, are of sufficient particularity to enable the appellants to answer in defence. However, this is not the only function of particulars. They also serve to narrow the issues for trial and to save time and expense in the trial preparation process and in the trial. In Lougheed v. C.B.C., [1979] 3 W.W.R. 334 at 352 … the Alberta Court of Appeal held: The defendant is entitled to such particulars as are reasonably necessary for its defence, both in respect of pleading and the steps leading to trial as well as the conduct of the trial itself. Mr. Justice Hope sets out an excellent summary of the purposes of providing particulars in Misericordia Hosp. v. Acres Consulting Services Ltd. (1977), 5 A.R. 254 at 255 (T.D.): In summary, those principles insofar as I see they apply to this application are: (a) The function of particulars is to limit the generality of allegations and define the issues to be tried—whereas examinations for discovery is to learn the knowledge of the adverse party; (b) Particulars do not include the facts within the knowledge of the applicant; (c) Particulars are not required to be given of the character of the act which it is alleged produced the damage nor the circumstances under which it is done; (d) A distinction is made between particulars of the ‘material fact’ stated generally in the Statement of Claim as ‘facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim’ and which he must state and particulars of the ‘evidence by which they are to be proved’. There is a fine line between providing sufficient particulars to enable a defendant to plead, and pleading evidence. The latter is specifically prohibited by R. 104, which states that the pleadings shall contain the material facts on which the party is relying, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved. In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 365-66, per Wachowich J. In Geophysical Service Incorporated v. Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55, 2021 CarswellAlta 278, the Court said: [5]“Particulars” are, by definition, further details about the claim originally pleaded. If they go beyond that, they are potentially “new” claims which must comply with s. 6(2). A plaintiff cannot indirectly add new claims to a proceeding by describing them as particulars. Further, if the particulars are merely evidence in support of the original claim, they are not a proper part of the pleading; pleadings are to allege facts, but not include evidence: R. 13.6(2)(a). 5. Particulars of Damages I will now deal with the issue of the particulars of damages. I agree with the submission by the defendants Clarkson Gordon and Peat Marwick that the plaintiffs must be required to give particulars of any special damages that they are claiming, so that the defendants are in a position to properly contest the quantum. According to Odgers' Principles of Pleadings and Practice, 22nd ed. (1981), p. 154: Particulars of general damages will very rarely be ordered. But when any special damage is claimed without sufficient detail, particulars will be ordered of the alleged damage, e.g. if the plaintiff alleges that certain customers have ceased to deal with him, he will be ordered to state their names. This is a very useful order, for if a plaintiff cannot give the names, he will be compelled to strike out the allegations of special damage; and the summons should ask that it be struck out if such particulars be not delivered. If he gives the necessary particulars he will be bound by them; he will not be allowed at the trial to give evidence of any special damage which is not claimed explicitly, either in his pleadings or particulars. If ambiguous expressions be used in the statement of claim which may or may not amount to allegations of special damage, the master will order ‘particulars of special damage, if any claimed.’ The first thing that must be considered, therefore, is whether the claim for $294,000,000 is for special or general damages. The distinction between special and general damages was laid down by Lord Macnaghten in Stroms Bruks Aktie Bolag v. Hutchinson, [1905] A.C. 515 at 525-56: ‘General damages’, as I understand the term, are such as the law will presume to be the direct, natural and probable consequence of the act complained of. ‘Special damages,’ on the other hand, are such as the law will not infer from the nature of the act. They do not follow in the ordinary course. They are exceptional in their character, and, therefore, they must be claimed specifically and proved strictly. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 at 369 (Q.B.).
